paper.title: Self-Modification of Policy and Utility Function in Rational Agents
paper.central_claim: Depending on how expected utility is computed (hedonistic, ignorant, realistic value functions), a rational agent able to modify its future policy or utility function either self-modifies harmfully or, if realistic, makes only essentially harmless modifications on-policy (Theorem 16).
paper.claim_type_note: No SCORE_SPEC claim_type (system_method / component_training / evaluation_resource) fits a pure formal-theory paper; left null because the disposition is out_of_scope. sol's 'system_method' misdescribes it; son55's 'unclassified_theory' is not an allowed value.

evidence.quote: We define formal models for two general kinds of self-modifications, where the agent can either change its future policy or its future utility function.
evidence.support_explanation: Self-modification is modelled abstractly as an action selecting the next policy/utility.

evidence.quote: abstracts away from most details of architecture and implementation
In this paper, we assumed that the agent knew the self-modifying consequences of its actions.
evidence.support_explanation: Consequences are given, not learned from execution feedback.

evidence.quote: shows that it is possible to create an agent that despite being able to make any self-modification will refrain from using it
evidence.support_explanation: Main result is about refraining from self-modification (goal preservation), not improving components.

evidence.quote: mainly by relaxing the assumption that the optimal policy only self-modifies if it has a strict incentive to do so
evidence.support_explanation: Contribution relative to Hibbard (2012): a relaxed assumption, re-proven.

evidence.quote: Our result only shows that the agent does not change its utility function
evidence.support_explanation: Does not cover tampering with the utility's inputs.

Searched all sections and Appendix A: no implementation, benchmark, experiment, executable component, feedback-driven edit or later-task measurement; results are theorems about optimal policies under three value-function definitions.

signatures.object: Future policy or utility function of an idealised agent (formal model).
signatures.information: Full history; known modification consequences; modification-independent belief.
signatures.operation: Optimal action selection under realistic/ignorant/hedonistic value functions where actions also select the next policy/utility.
signatures.output: Theorems on when optimal agents self-modify.
signatures.conditions: Perfect rationality, explicit modification consequences, discounted bounded utility.
signatures.feedback: Percepts in the formal model; no learning from execution feedback.
signatures.persistence: Selected policy/utility governs the next step (formal).
signatures.claimed_effect: Goal preservation for realistic agents (safety), not performance improvement.
signatures.failure_boundary: On-policy only; utility-input tampering not covered; corrigibility, value learning and exploration issues noted.

gap.author_gap: Hibbard (2012) only established that an optimal non-modifying policy exists; safety needs all optimal policies to be non-harmful.
gap.checked_gap: A theory gap within AI-safety decision theory; not a gap about feedback-driven non-weight self-improvement.
lineage: Orseau & Ring 2011; Gödel machine (cited, not pinned)
gap.stakes: Background for evaluator/goal drift in self-modifying systems.
gap.method_response: Formal separation of three value-function types with proofs.
gap.remaining_gap: Not evaluated further: out of scope.
